Now, I leave not only with a solid foundation in this sacred tradition but with a heart full of warmth, gratitude, and memories that will linger like the scent of the herbal balls we made 😄. It is a complex scent that will always remind me of the wonderful time we all have spent together.

I'm grateful to have met the kindest and most generous souls who not only taught us massage skills but also how to respect and take care of each other as a family, how to enjoy life, how to find a balance within the nuances of life itself and everything else that matters.

Chiang Mai and the Old Medicine Hospital have etched themselves into my soul — a place of peace, kindness, and timeless wisdom. They will forever hold a special place in my heart.

text:
While there are tons of massage parlors in town, I decided to try a treatment at a long-established school.

It was so relaxing that I ended up booking another one the following week.

A 90-minute herbal compress for 600 baht.
The massage uses large steamed herbal balls to massage my entire body.
The treatment is performed by a teacher from the school, so I'm sure they're skilled.

After changing into my treatment attire, I lie face down, and the teacher, holding the herbal ball, says a prayer before starting.

The heat from the herbal ball gently spreads down my back, feeling so good I can't help but let out the same sigh I get when I enter a hot spring.

The herbal ball is applied directly to my skin or over my treatment attire, and as the temperature drops, I change out for a new warm herbal ball as I massage.

The relaxing herbal scent, the warm heat, the medicinal properties of the herbs, and the therapist's skilled technique combine to melt away the fatigue of travel.

The stomach massage was especially pleasant, as my stomach and intestines, tired from all the food I'd had on my trip, were gently kneaded and soothed.
It reminded me of the happy feeling of my mother gently washing my body in a warm bath.

I can't get this experience in Japan, so it makes me want to go back to Chiang Mai.

There's also a herbal steam sauna next door.

Please note:
When using the herbal compress, your shorts will be stained with the yellow turmeric, so make sure you wear shorts that you don't mind getting stained.
Your body will also turn a little yellow.

Update:

Old Medicine Hospital – reflections and recommendations for future students

I attended several courses at Old Medicine Hospital, drawn by its historical significance and its role in the preservation and dissemination of traditional Thai medicine. The school has a special atmosphere and a warm environment, and it’s clear that students from all over the world come with curiosity and an open mind.

That said, I’d like to share a few observations that may be helpful for future students:

In one of the courses, we were issued a Tok Sen toolset – a traditional instrument with deep roots in Thai therapeutic practice. I was surprised that the teacher brought in to lead the class neither used nor acknowledged the standard toolset provided by the school – which ultimately holds responsibility for the course content. She openly stated that she was unfamiliar with the tools, which also raises concerns about her familiarity with the school’s curriculum. Instead, she offered to sell her own set for 1,500 baht, even though a similar set could be purchased outside the school for around 450–550 baht. I don’t mind paying a bit more for good equipment, but it becomes problematic when you join a course where the instructor doesn’t know the tools provided and simultaneously promotes her own for sale. It felt like an unfortunate blend of teaching and personal business.

It is also noteworthy that Tok Sen is one of the few subjects at the school without any kind of examination or formal assessment, unlike other programs. Given Old Medicine Hospital’s status as a cultural institution and authority within traditional Thai medicine, it seems particularly odd that this valuable heritage practice is treated with such minimal emphasis.

Examinations in the other subjects are oral, and students are allowed to use their notes, which is appreciated. However, I experienced some inconsistency in how the use of materials was evaluated. In one course, using the textbook was not an issue; in another, it was considered a negative – even though I approached both in the same way.

Teaching is generally structured around students practicing on each other, which can be a great learning method. Instructors are present, but their supervision tends to focus on what the techniques look like, rather than how they feel to the receiver. This means that important sensory aspects of the work can easily be missed.

If you’re considering taking multiple courses in Thai bodywork, I strongly recommend spreading them across different schools. Each school offers a unique approach, and some provide the opportunity to practice on teachers or models who are familiar with the techniques – which makes a big difference in understanding what the methods should truly feel like.

All in all, Old Medicine Hospital offers a historical setting and can be a valuable starting point – especially if you come with curiosity and a willingness to take responsibility for your own learning. By asking specific questions before enrolling – such as about the use of materials, exam structure, and the level of supervision – you can make the most of your experience.

text:
My intention in writing this review is to honestly share my experience so others can make informed decisions before enrolling.

1. If your goal is to take a BASIC course and/or have FUN and a NEW EXPERIENCE, this is the PLACE for you. It's a very flexible place, with very basic knowledge.

2. If your intention is to have IN-DEPTH and HIGH-QUALITY learning, this school is not for you.

The positives, superficially:

1. They give you a shirt upon completing levels 1-2 and pants upon completing levels 3-4.

2. They provide coffee, tea, and cookies or snacks at the cafe counter.

3. Food is available to order there, so you don't waste time looking for somewhere to eat.

4. At level 3, after the Herbal Compress, you can enter the steam room and experience Herbal Steam.

The rest:
Marketing name: The prestige of being the first Thai Massage school in the north. As a comment, they could maintain the same traditional essence while improving the quality of the support materials and infrastructure. If they were pioneers in the past, they should continue to be so. I feel they're stuck with what worked and won't budge from it. I was surprised that Thai people choose not to attend, but now I understand.

Methodology: They give you a basic book (attached), and you have to write and watch the teacher's demonstration simultaneously. Not everyone expects you to write, and not everyone explains well. In practice, many teachers don't correct you unless you raise your hand and interrupt their conversation with groups more interested in talking than practicing. The groups are large, and there's not enough space to properly observe the demonstration. If the teacher does something with their back to you, you'll hardly find space on the other side, given how many people there are. In theory, they should demonstrate from both sides. At some levels, you can't record; it relies on your ability to quickly and accurately describe what you observe. In my case, I can't really describe it, haha, and my notes were terrible, so I suffered quite a bit when I was practicing and they would tell me, "Read your notes," and then go back to talking.
Their explanation for the methodology is that "we learn more by writing."

1. Poor infrastructure
2. Lack of professionalism and humiliating attitudes from the teachers, with the exception of a couple.

3. Administrative shortcomings, LACK OF PROFESSIONALISM and seriousness: I have two certificates. One for 60 hours of Thai Massage and another for 180 hours of Thai Therapeutic Massage. They gave me an extra 60 hours on the certificate.
Lack of alignment between the two administrators; when you point out prior agreements or errors in the information being interpreted, they minimize you. The woman disparaged her colleague.

4. Certification without merit, payment for receiving a "participation" certificate or purchased title: They hand out the certificate even if you don't master the technique at all, your maneuvers are very dangerous, or you've missed several hours of class. This contradicts their own internal regulations.

5. Poor support material: Basic photos that don't show the step-by-step process, with drawings that are barely visible. The images don't always match the content covered in class. Level 4, the material includes huge illustrations that aren't useful for practice; you have to draw your own, but there's no space for that—everything is covered with lines for you to write on.

6. Unfulfilled hours: They don't meet the established hours. 1-3 hours per day are not completed. The start time is always late, with the end time being early. In the end, you lose seriousness and commitment to the course because of the constant disorganization. It's just fun, very relaxed.

7. Quantity over quality. "The prices are low," they claim.
